source_text: Quaestionem rursus de curatione sabbatis facta quomodo discussit? unusquisque uestrum sabbatis non soluits asinum aut bouem suum a praesepi et ducit ad potum? ergo secundum condicionem legis operatus legem confirmauit, non dissoluit, iubentem nullum opus fieri, nisi quod fieret omni animae, quanto potius humanae? Parabolarum congruentiam ubique recognoscor exigere. simile est regnum dei, inquit, grano sinapis, quod accepit homo et seminauit in horto suo. quis in persona hominis intellegendus? utique Christus, qui, licet Marcionis, filius hominis est dictus, qui accepit a patre semen regni, sermonem scilicet euangelii, et seminauit in horto, isto utique in mundo. puta nunc in homine, sed cum in (suo) horto dixerit nec mundus autem nec homo illius sit, sed creatoris, ergo qui in suum seminarit creatoris ostenditur. aut si, ut hunc laqueum euadant, conuerterint hominis personam a Christo in hominem accipientem semen regni et seminantem in horto cordis sui, nec ipsa materia alii conueniet quam creatori.
pass_a_gloss: The question of the healing on the Sabbath, how did he discuss it? Does not each one of you on the Sabbath untie his donkey or ox from the manger and lead it to water? Therefore, according to the condition of the law, he operated the law, he confirmed it, not dissolved it, commanding that no work be done, except what would be done for every soul, how much more for a human one? I recognize that the congruence of parables is required everywhere. The kingdom of God, he says, is similar to a grain of mustard, which a man received and sowed in his garden. Who is to be understood in the person of the man? Certainly Christ, who, even if according to Marcion, is called the son of man, who received from the Father the seed of the kingdom, namely the sermon of the gospel, and sowed it in the garden, certainly in this world. Suppose now in the man, but since when he says in his garden, neither the world nor the man is his, but the creator's, therefore he who sows in his own is shown to be the creator's. Or if, in order to escape this snare, they turn the person of the man from Christ to a man receiving the seed of the kingdom and sowing it in the garden of his heart, not even this matter will be suitable for anyone other than the creator.

who is to be understood in the person of the man
rejected: who is the man to be understood as

bible_refs.note: similar parable about the kingdom of God and the mustard seed

pass_b_english: How did he take apart the question of the Sabbath cure? "Doesn't each of you on the Sabbath untie his donkey or ox from the manger and lead it to water?" (Matthew 12:11). So, working within the law's own terms, he confirmed the law instead of abolishing it—the law that commands no work be done except what serves any living soul, how much more a human one? I see that parables must match up at every point. "The kingdom of God is like a mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden" (Luke 13:18-19; Mark 4:30-32). Who is the "man"? Clearly Christ, who even on Marcion's terms is called the Son of Man. He received the kingdom's seed—the gospel message—from the Father and sowed it in his garden, this world. Now suppose the "man" is a human being; but when Jesus says "his garden," neither the world nor the man belongs to him—both belong to the Creator. So the one who sows in his own garden is shown to be the Creator's. Or if, to dodge this trap, they shift the "man" from Christ to a human who receives the kingdom's seed and sows it in the garden of his heart, even that scenario fits no one but the Creator.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that correctly incorporates the necessary scripture citations (Matthew 12:11, Luke 13:18-19, Mark 4:30-32) for the quoted/alluded parables. The distinction between the 'man' as Christ and the 'man' as a human (to avoid the 'snare') is preserved in both.
